'''''Rosa banksiae''''', [[common name]]s '''Lady Banks' rose''', or just '''Banks' rose''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the rose [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[native plant|native]] to central and western China, in the provinces of Gansu, Guizhou, Henan, Hubei, Jiangsu, Sichuan and Yunnan, at altitudes of {{cvt|500|-|2200|m|ft|-2}}.<ref name=efloras/> The rose is named for [[Lady Dorothea Banks|Dorothea Lady Banks]], the wife of botanist [[Joseph Banks|Sir Joseph Banks]].

==Description==
[[File:SsSsگل.JPG|thumb|220px|Blooming flowers|left]]
It is a scrambling [[shrub]]by [[vine]] growing vigorously to {{cvt|6|m|ft|0}} tall. Unlike most roses, it is practically [[spine (botany)|thornless]], though it may bear some prickles up to 5 mm long, particularly on stout, strong shoots. The [[leaf|leaves]] are [[evergreen]], 4–6 cm long, with three to five (rarely seven) [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]] 2–5 cm long with a serrated margin.

The flowers are small, 1.5–2.5 cm diameter, white or pale yellow and are fragrant. It is amongst the earliest flowering of all roses, usually appearing during May in the northern hemisphere, though cold weather can delay flowering.<ref name=RHSAZ/> All Lady Banks' roses are said to smell of [[Viola (plant)|violets]] to varying degrees.<ref>Charlotte Testu The old roses, Paris, The Rustic house - Flammarion1984 ({{ISBN|2-7066-0139-6}}), p.  185.</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Rosa banksiae'' was first described and published by W. T. Aiton in '[[Hortus Kewensis|Hortus kew.]]' edition 2, Vol.3 on page 258 in 1811.<ref name="grin">{{cite web |title=Taxonomy - GRIN-Global Web v 1.10.6.2 |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=70574 |website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov |access-date=17 May 2020 }}</ref> Some places attribute [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] as the author <ref name="plantlist"/> but it was agreed in 2018 by [[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|ICN]] that W. T. Aiton was the true author.<ref name="grin"/>

==Cultivation and uses==
''Rosa banksiae'' has likely been grown in the gardens of China for hundreds of years. The species was introduced to Europe by [[William Kerr (gardener)|William Kerr]], who had been sent on a plant-hunting expedition by Sir Joseph Banks. He bought the first Lady Banks' Rose, subsequently named the white Lady Banks (''R. banksiae'' var. ''banksiae'') from the famous [[Fa Tee]] nursery in 1807.<ref name=Old>Graham Murphy {{google books|nYw77SS8HfQC Old Roses (2003)|page=26 }}</ref>

A number of other forms were subsequently discovered growing in China, including ''R. banksiae'' var. ''normalis'' (see above), and ''R. banksiae'' 'Lutea', the yellow Lady Banks' rose (brought to Europe in 1824 by J. D. Parks). In 1993 this [[cultivar]] earned the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name=RHSlist/> It is used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]], with portions of other plants and herbs (such as [[monkshood]] and ''[[Ligusticum wallichii]]'') to make a [[liniment]] to treat a painful swelling of the joints.<ref>{{cite web |title=It is a kind of to be used to treat liniment of painful swelling of joints and preparation method thereof |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/CN107349268A/en |access-date=24 May 2020 |language=en |date=15 July 2017 }}</ref>

An ''R. banksiae'' planted in [[Tombstone, Arizona]] in 1885 is reputedly the world's largest rose bush. It covers up to {{convert|9000|sqft|m2}} of the roof on an inn, and has a {{convert|12|ft|m|adj=on}} circumference trunk.<ref name=NPR/>

===Varieties===
There were several [[variety (biology)|varieties]] named, none of which are currently accepted. Among these are:<ref name=efloras/><ref name="POWO_731723-1" >{{cite POWO |id=731723-1 |title=''Rosa banksiae'' W.T.Aiton |access-date=30 August 2025 }}</ref>
*''Rosa banksiae'' var. ''banksiae'' – flowers semi-double or double, with numerous petals replacing most or all of the [[stamen]]s; a [[cultigen]] developed in Chinese gardens
*''Rosa banksiae'' var. ''flava''
*''Rosa banksiae'' var. ''inermis''
*''Rosa banksiae'' var. ''lutea''
*''Rosa banksiae'' var. ''normalis'' – flowers single, with five petals; said to be the natural wild form of the species
*''Rosa banksiae'' var. ''plena''
